subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 22-year-old college sprinter collapses after a 400-m race with severe leg fatigue and is helped off the track. He is well hydrated, his heart rate is 118/min, and his blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Ten minutes after the race, venous lactate is 13.8 mmol/L and pyruvate is mildly elevated with an anion gap of 22. The next morning his lactate is normal.
question: During his race, which of the following enzymes most directly permitted continued anaerobic glycolysis in his skeletal muscle by regenerating NAD+?
explanation_correct: The glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction requires NAD+ and reduces it to NADH, so glycolysis stops unless NAD+ is regenerated. In skeletal muscle, lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate in the cytosol, oxidizing NADH back to NAD+ and permitting ATP production to continue at 2 net ATP per glucose when mitochondria cannot keep pace with demand. The lactate is later cleared by the liver through the Cori cycle.

explanation_incorrect.A: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is mitochondrial and would consume pyruvate oxidatively; it does not regenerate cytosolic NAD+ and cannot support high flux in this setting.
explanation_incorrect.B: Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate in the mitochondrial matrix for gluconeogenesis and anaplerosis; it uses ATP and biotin and does not regenerate NAD+.
explanation_incorrect.C: Alanine aminotransferase transfers the amino group of alanine to alpha-ketoglutarate and does not regenerate NAD+ for glycolysis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase itself consumes NAD+ and produces NADH; it is the step that requires regeneration, not the source of it.

educationalObjective: Lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate to lactate, allowing anaerobic glycolysis and ATP production to continue in skeletal muscle.
